Filename: 2020 Groenke, Monteleoni - ClimAlign - Unsupervised statistical downscaling of climate variables via normalizing flows.pdf
Title: ClimAlign: Unsupervised statistical downscaling of climate variables via normalizing flows
Venue: 10th International Conference on Climate Informatics (CI2020), ACM
Model family (as reported): normalizing flow (AlignFlow: Glow-based flows with adversarial/Wasserstein critic loss)
Variable(s): daily maximum temperature; daily precipitation
Data source: ERA-Interim (low-res input) and WRF regional climate model output (high-res target); second experiment uses NOAA 20th Century Reanalysis (NOAA20CR) and Livneh gridded observations
Grid size: Low-res ~1deg (ERA-Interim, NOAA20CR); high-res 1/4deg (WRF-4) and 1/8deg (Livneh, from native ~1/16deg)
N_train: Not given as a sample count; ERA-I/WRF-4 experiment uses a sliding training window of 4018 days (~11 yrs) per CV fold from a total 4748-day (~13 yr) dataset; NOAA20CR/Livneh experiment trains on 1987-1999 (13 yrs)
N_eval: ERA-I/WRF-4: held-out test set of last 730 days (2 yrs), evaluated across 5 folds of 146 days each; NOAA20CR/Livneh: evaluated on 2000-2013 (14 yrs)
Leakage notes: Uses 5-fold time-series cross-validation with an explicit sliding training window and a chronologically later holdout test block (last 730 days); the NOAA20CR/Livneh experiment also uses non-overlapping time periods (1987-1999 train vs 2000-2013 test). No random shuffling of days is used.
Q1a notes (metric used): Climdex indices (monthly bias for TXx/TXn; correlation for CDD/CWD/Rx1d/Rx5d/SDII) computed between predicted and observed fields (Tables 1-2); Table 4 also reports climatological bias at specific percentiles (Mean, P50, P98, P02) for precipitation.
Q1b notes: No histogram/PDF-overlay-only comparison; all distributional claims are backed by the quantified Climdex/percentile-bias metrics above. Figure 3 shows a time-series line plot as a supplementary visual, not a substitute for quantification.
Q1c notes: No spatial power-spectrum or spectral analysis of any kind is reported.
Q1d notes: Climdex extreme/occurrence indices (TXx, TXn, CDD, CWD, Rx1d, Rx5d, SDII) and percentile-based climatological bias (P98, P02) are dedicated extremes evaluations beyond RMSE/bias/correlation.
Q2a notes: RMSE, bias and correlation are computed per grid location conditioned on the low-resolution input (Tables 1-3), i.e. per-condition pointwise stats, but only for the deterministic/maximum-likelihood prediction; the stochastic conditional-sampling capability (Eq. 8) is never quantitatively scored.
Q2b notes: No PIT/rank histogram, spread-error, or reliability diagram is reported; variance across conditional samples (sigma=0.7) is discussed only qualitatively ('a realistic amount of variance').
Q3 notes: No checks for physical bounds/non-negativity of precipitation, conservation, or other structural constraints on individual generated samples are reported.
Q4a notes (metric used): No quantitative diversity/coverage metric; latent-space Slerp interpolation (Fig. 2) and conditional sample panels (Fig. 1) are qualitative/visual demonstrations only.
Q4b notes: No comparison of generated samples to nearest neighbors in the training set; memorization is not addressed.
Q5a notes: The AlignFlow critic networks (cX, cY) are used only inside the adversarial training loss (WGAN-style), not as a post-hoc two-sample test on held-out real vs. generated samples.
Q5b notes: No train-on-synthetic-test-on-real or augmentation-gain experiment is performed.
V1 notes: No sensitivity check (metric response to a degraded input) or non-gameability control against a statistic-matched null baseline is reported.
U1 notes: Tables 1-2 report metric mean +/- standard deviation across the 5 time-series CV folds, giving a resampling-based uncertainty estimate on RMSE/bias/correlation.
U2 notes: No real-vs-real 'floor' quantity (e.g., split-half or observational-uncertainty baseline) is computed.
B1 notes: BCSD (bias-correction spatial disaggregation), a quantile-mapping/interpolation statistical downscaling method, is used as a non-ML baseline alongside supervised BMD-CNN.
R1 notes: "Both the implementation used for this work and the baselines used for comparison are available on GitHub" (https://github.com/bgroenks96/generative-downscaling).
R2 notes: The 5-fold time-series CV protocol (fold sizes, sliding-window lengths) is described in detail, but no random seeds are reported and some evaluation parameters (e.g., the precipitation threshold epsilon in the sparse-error metric) are not fully specified.
Notable practices (free text): Uses genuine temporal (time-series) cross-validation with explicit sliding-window blocks and reports fold-to-fold standard deviations on its error metrics, which is good practice rarely seen in this literature. However, essentially all quantitative evaluation targets the deterministic/maximum-likelihood prediction; the model's headline capability -- probabilistic conditional and unconditional sampling -- is only illustrated visually (a handful of sample panels and a latent-space interpolation), never scored with a distributional, calibration, or diversity metric.
Memorable unquantified-similarity quotes: "While each conditional sample is still similar to the maximum likelihood prediction, there appears to be a realistic amount of variance across the samples in where the precipitation events occur." (Section 4.1) "For both temperature and precipitation, the figure demonstrates that interpolation in the latent space results in a smooth transition between the two real samples, with only the relevant spatial features being affected." (Section 4.1)
QC method applied: Sample spot-check only (3/41 papers independently re-verified; not per-paper)

Filename: 2020 Leinonen - Stochastic Super-Resolution for Downscaling Time-Evolving Atmospheric Fields with a Generative Adversarial Network.pdf
Title: Stochastic Super-Resolution for Downscaling Time-Evolving Atmospheric Fields With a Generative Adversarial Network
Venue: IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing, Vol. 59, No. 9, September 2021 (published online Nov. 2020)
Model family (as reported): Conditional recurrent GAN, trained as a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP); CNN generator/discriminator built from residual blocks plus convolutional gated recurrent units (ConvGRU) for temporal consistency
Variable(s): Precipitation rate R (mm/h, log-transformed) from ground radar; cloud optical thickness τ (log-transformed) from GOES-16 satellite
Data source: MeteoSwiss ground-based weather radar composite (MCH-RZC, Switzerland, year 2018) and GOES-16 (GOES-R series) satellite-derived cloud optical thickness (GOES-COT, Apr-Dec 2019); both are real observational remote-sensing products, not model simulations
Grid size: High-resolution 128x128 pixels (1 km/pixel MCH-RZC, 2 km/pixel GOES-COT); low-resolution conditioning input 8x8 pixels (16x super-resolution factor); 8 time frames per sequence at 10-min intervals. Fully convolutional/recurrent architecture later applied post-training to much larger domains (704x640 pixels) and much longer sequences (3-month time series).
N_train: MCH-RZC: 180,000 total 8-frame sequences (2018), 90% used for training; generator trained on 400,000 sampled sequences (3.2M images), discriminator on 2,000,000 sequences (10M images). GOES-COT: 108,544 total sequences (2019), same 90/10 split and training regime.
N_eval: 10% of each dataset (~18,000 MCH-RZC / ~10,854 GOES-COT sequences) held out as a validation set; separate test sets of 1024 sequences each drawn from a different time period (MCH-RZC: year 2017; GOES-COT: April 1-20, 2020); rank/variability statistics computed using ensembles of 100 GAN realizations per sample.
Leakage notes: The reported test sets are explicitly temporally block-separated (different year/period entirely from training: 2017 vs. 2018 for radar; a different 2020 window vs. 2019 training period for GOES), which is good practice and low-leakage. However, the validation set (also reported in Table I and used to monitor/select the training checkpoint) was formed by "randomly selecting" 10% of sequences from the same year as training, with no stated temporal blocking; since 10-min-interval radar/satellite sequences are strongly autocorrelated, nearby-in-time sequences could appear in both the training and validation pools, making the validation-based metrics (and checkpoint selection based on them) potentially leakage-prone even though the headline test-set generalization claim is not.
Q1a notes (metric used): No quantitative comparison of the marginal/bulk distribution of the physical variable itself (e.g., a rainfall-rate or cloud-optical-thickness PDF/CDF compared via a distance or divergence) is reported. The reported metrics (RMSE, MS-SSIM, LSD, CRPS) are pixel-wise image-quality/ensemble scores, not two-sample distributional comparisons of the field values.
Q1b notes: No histogram/PDF overlay of the physical field's values (rain rate or cloud optical thickness) is shown anywhere; comparisons are via example image panels (Figs. 2, 3, 7) and quantitative image/ensemble metrics, not distribution plots.
Q1c notes: The log spectral distance (LSD, Eq. 7) quantifies the difference (in dB) between the power spectra of real and generated images; it is tracked during training (Fig. 4) and reported numerically in Table I, and the GAN is shown to substantially outperform Lanczos/RCNN/RainFARM baselines on this metric.
Q1d notes: No dedicated analysis of extremes/tails (e.g., exceedance frequencies, extreme percentiles of rain rate or COT) is performed; the outlier fraction (OF) metric concerns ensemble-rank outliers (calibration), not the tail of the physical variable's distribution.
Q2a notes: CRPS (continuous ranked probability score, a strictly proper score, Eq. 10) is computed per pixel/image and tracked over training and reported in Table I, directly assessing the fidelity of the conditional predictive ensemble against the single ground truth per input.
Q2b notes: A rank-histogram/Talagrand-diagram approach adapted from ensemble weather forecasting is used (Section II-D): pixel-wise normalized rank r of the truth within a 100-member ensemble is examined visually (Fig. 6 histogram and CDF) and quantified via the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, Kullback-Leibler divergence, outlier fraction, and mean-rank bias (Fig. 5, Table I) versus the ideal uniform distribution.
Q3 notes: No explicit post-hoc check of physical admissibility (e.g., verifying that averaging the generated HR field recovers the LR conditioning input, mass/energy conservation, or systematic non-negativity/bounds checking across the ensemble) is reported. Value range [0,1] is only enforced by construction (sigmoid output layer), not evaluated. The paper does note (Section IV-E, Appendix) that the recurrent generator can produce artifacts over long autoregressive runs and describes an ad hoc state-relaxation fix, but this is identified subjectively/qualitatively rather than via a quantified admissibility metric.
Q4a notes (metric used): The authors explicitly frame the rank-statistics analysis (KS, KL divergence, outlier fraction, mean-rank bias, Section II-D/IV-C) as a test of whether "the GAN produces close to the correct amount of variability in its outputs," i.e., a quantitative diversity/coverage check of the ensemble spread, in addition to its role in calibration (Q2b). They also note FID (the standard diversity metric for unconditional GANs) is explicitly considered but rejected as inapplicable to this conditional, single-truth-per-input setting.
Q4b notes: No nearest-neighbor or similarity search between generated samples and the training set is performed. The paper only states the general intention ("to ensure that we avoid the scenario where the GAN simply memorizes the training set, we set aside 10% of samples... as validation set") and relies on generalization to a temporally distinct test set (2017/2020) as indirect evidence against memorization, without an explicit memorization check.
Q5a notes: The adversarial discriminator is used only as part of the WGAN-GP training objective; no independent, held-out classifier-based two-sample test (C2ST) is used as a post-hoc evaluation metric on the trained generator's outputs.
Q5b notes: No downstream task (e.g., train-on-synthetic/test-on-real, hydrological impact metric, or other applied task) is evaluated; the paper is limited to image-quality/ensemble-calibration metrics and visual comparison.
V1 notes: Two forms of metric-validity checking appear. (1) Sensitivity: the authors tune the input noise amplitude (0.5x-3.0x) and observe that for under-trained generators this "could significantly improve the variability metrics," i.e., the rank-based metrics respond as expected to a controlled change in actual output variability (Section IV-C). (2) Non-gameability/limitation check: comparison against deterministic baselines (Lanczos, RMSE-trained RCNN) shows RMSE and MS-SSIM give similar (non-discriminating) scores for the GAN and for smooth deterministic methods, which the authors use to explicitly argue "these are not particularly good metrics for evaluating GAN performance as they penalize solutions with higher variance" (Section IV-D) — i.e., an explicit demonstration that some of their own candidate metrics fail to reward realistic variability.
U1 notes: All reported metrics (Table I; Figs. 4-6) are single point estimates or training-curve traces; no confidence intervals, bootstrap resampling, or error bars are computed for RMSE, MS-SSIM, LSD, CRPS, KS, KL divergence, or outlier fraction.
U2 notes: No real-vs-real reference/floor (e.g., a split-half or independent-realization comparison of the observational data itself, or a sampling-noise baseline) is computed; all comparisons are GAN/baseline-vs-truth.
B1 notes: RainFARM (Rebora et al.'s rainfall filtered autoregressive model, a traditional statistical stochastic downscaling method based on power-law spectral scaling of Gaussian random fields) and Lanczos interpolation (a traditional non-ML image-scaling method) are both used as baselines in Section IV-D and Table I, alongside a deterministic RMSE-trained RCNN (ML baseline with noise disabled).
R1 notes: "The source code to our GAN is available at https://github.com/jleinonen/downscaling-rnn-gan" (Abstract, Section II-B). The MCH-RZC training dataset is also cited as publicly released via Harvard Dataverse (ref. [50]).
R2 notes: Substantial protocol detail is given for reproducing the evaluation: exact test-set sizes/periods (1024 sequences, specific date ranges), the checkpoint used for headline figures (361,600/371,200 training sequences), the number of ensemble members for rank statistics (100), and closed-form metric definitions (Eqs. 6-10). However, no explicit random seed is reported for training or for ensemble/noise sampling during evaluation, so exact numerical reproduction would rely on the released code/data rather than a stated seed.
Notable practices (free text): Good practice: the authors explicitly recognize that FID (the standard GAN diversity metric) is inapplicable to their single-truth-per-input conditional setting and instead import rank-histogram/Talagrand-diagram and CRPS verification tools from ensemble weather forecasting — a methodologically thoughtful, discipline-appropriate substitute that is both visualized and quantified (KS, KL divergence, outlier fraction). They also explicitly show that RMSE/MS-SSIM fail to discriminate the GAN from blurrier deterministic baselines, a useful metric-limitation caveat rather than cherry-picking favorable metrics. Weaknesses: no physical-admissibility checks (e.g., LR-consistency/conservation checks on the super-resolved field), no memorization/nearest-neighbor check, no uncertainty quantification on any reported metric, and the validation split (as opposed to the temporally separate test split) is a random 10% draw from the same year without stated temporal blocking despite highly autocorrelated 10-minute sequences.
Memorable unquantified-similarity quotes: "We find that the GAN can generate realistic, temporally consistent super-resolution sequences for both data sets." (Abstract). "The examples illustrate that GAN produces more detail and more visually accurate reconstruction of the original image than the alternative methods." (Section IV-D, Comparison to Alternative Methods). "The GAN, on the other hand, works quite robustly and very rarely generates any implausible artifacts." (Section IV-D). "At the top, all three reconstructions produce a similar, uniform structure that strongly resembles the texture of the original." (Section IV-A, describing Fig. 2).
QC method applied: Per-paper adversarial verify (model_family/Q4a/Q4b/U2/V1/eligibility) — papers_second_batch

Filename: 2020 Mooers, Beucler - Generative Modeling of Atmospheric Convection.pdf
Title: Generative Modeling of Atmospheric Convection
Venue: 10th International Conference on Climate Informatics (CI2020), ACM
Model family (as reported): VAE (including a covariance-constrained variant, 'CC-VAE')
Variable(s): vertical velocity (convective-scale, 30 vertical levels x 128 CRM columns)
Data source: Cloud-resolving model (SAM) embedded in the Super-Parameterized CAM5 (SPCAM5) global climate model; simulated tropical-belt (20N-20S) output
Grid size: 30 vertical levels x 128 CRM columns (padded to 32x128 as network input)
N_train: 111,206 snapshots (80% of a 4.3Gb class-balanced dataset drawn from an initial ~1.3Tb / ~6x10^6-sample pool)
N_eval: 27,802 snapshots (20% held-out test split)
Leakage notes: The paper states data are 'shuffled in the spatial and temporal dimensions prior to training' before the 80/20 split, i.e. the split unit is individual snapshots rather than spatial or temporal blocks; since CRM snapshots are output every 15 minutes at neighboring grid columns, strong spatiotemporal autocorrelation between train and test snapshots is likely and is not addressed.
Q1a notes (metric used): Hellinger distance H(p,q) between the distributions of true vs. reconstructed vertical velocity fields is reported quantitatively (Table 3), along with MSE and a Frobenius-norm covariance-matrix error.
Q1b notes: Distributional comparisons are quantified (Hellinger distance, Frobenius norm); Figure 4's visual reconstruction panel is supplementary to, not a replacement for, these metrics.
Q1c notes: One-dimensional power spectral density (Eq. 5) is computed at 4 vertical levels (850/700/500/250 hPa) for truth, VAE, CC-VAE and the linear baseline and plotted quantitatively (Figure 2).
Q1d notes: ELBO is used to flag anomalous/extreme storm snapshots (Fig. 6) as a use-case demonstration, but there is no quantitative comparison of tail statistics (e.g. extreme percentiles) between true and reconstructed/generated distributions.
Q2a notes: Task is unconditional reconstruction/representation learning, not conditional generation on an external input field.
Q2b notes: Task is unconditional; no probabilistic conditional forecast is produced to calibrate.
Q3 notes: No explicit physical-admissibility check (e.g. bounds on vertical velocity magnitude, continuity) of individual reconstructed fields; the covariance-constraint loss shapes training but is not used as a post-hoc validity check.
Q4a notes (metric used): The Frobenius-norm covariance-matching metric (Table 3) quantifies how well the variance/covariance structure of reconstructions matches the true data (a spread-fidelity proxy), but there is no explicit diversity/coverage metric across multiple generated samples per input, since the study is a reconstruction/representation-learning task rather than multi-sample generation.
Q4b notes: No nearest-neighbor-to-training-set comparison is performed to assess memorization.
Q5a notes: No classifier-based two-sample test is used.
Q5b notes: No downstream task-utility experiment beyond illustrative anomaly-detection/clustering demonstrations, which are not benchmarked against a task metric.
V1 notes: Comparing Linear/VAE/CC-VAE (Table 3) shows the Frobenius-norm and Hellinger metrics vary meaningfully with model quality (e.g. three-orders-of-magnitude difference in covariance Frobenius norm between Linear and CC-VAE), incidentally suggesting metric sensitivity to model differences, but there is no deliberate corrupted/null-baseline control designed to validate the metrics.
U1 notes: Table 3 reports single point values for MSE/Hellinger distance/Frobenius norm with no confidence intervals or bootstrap resampling.
U2 notes: No real-vs-real reference/floor quantity is computed.
B1 notes: A 'linear' autoencoder baseline (identity activations, MSE loss -- effectively a linear/PCA-type model) is used for comparison (Table 3), but this is a trained network, not a classical climatology/persistence/analog baseline.
R1 notes: "The code for this study can be found at https://github.com/gmooers96/CBRAIN-CAM/tree/master/MAPS".
R2 notes: Architecture, preprocessing, and the 80/20 split are described in detail, but no random seeds are reported.
Notable practices (free text): Quantifies reconstruction fidelity via Hellinger distance, MSE, and covariance Frobenius-norm error, and performs genuine multi-level spectral analysis rather than relying on visual PDF comparison alone -- a relatively rigorous set of physically-motivated metrics for a short workshop paper. However, the train/test split is done on randomly shuffled spatiotemporal snapshots (not spatial or temporal blocks) despite the data being high-frequency (15-min) CRM output, creating an undiscussed leakage risk; there is also no assessment of memorization, sample diversity, or calibration since the model is used mainly for reconstruction/representation learning and anomaly detection rather than generating novel stochastic realizations.
Memorable unquantified-similarity quotes: "The trained VAE reconstructions closely resemble those from the test dataset and accurately predict the location, magnitude and spatial structure of convective plumes." (Figure 4 caption, p.102) -- asserted from a single visual example without a metric tied specifically to that figure.
QC method applied: Sample spot-check only (3/41 papers independently re-verified; not per-paper)

Filename: 2020 Stengel - Adversarial super-resolution of climatological wind and solar data.pdf
Title: Adversarial super-resolution of climatological wind and solar data
Venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), vol. 117, no. 29, pp. 16805-16815
Model family (as reported): Conditional GAN (SRGAN-based, modified: no batch normalization; two-step cascaded super-resolution generator [LR->MR then MR->HR], each with pretrained-CNN stage then adversarial fine-tuning stage, plus a discriminator network)
Variable(s): Near-surface wind velocity components (u,v; 100-m height in WIND Toolkit training data, lowest sigma-pressure level in CCSM) and solar irradiance (direct normal irradiance [DNI] and diffuse horizontal irradiance [DHI], derived from CCSM downwelling shortwave/GHI via a decomposition model for the CCSM application case)
Data source: Training/validation/test HR data: NREL WIND Toolkit (wind, 2007-2013, continental US) and NREL National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) (solar, 2007-2013, continental US), coarsened to create LR/MR/HR training pairs. Application/deployment (no ground truth) data: NCAR CCSM4 output for CMIP5 "1% per year CO2" scenario (2020-2039).
Grid size: LR (CCSM): 0.9 deg lat x 1.25 deg lon (~100 km). Intermediate MR: 10 km (wind) / 20 km (solar). HR: 2 km (WIND Toolkit wind) / 4 km (NSRDB solar), i.e. 50x and 25x resolution enhancement respectively. Training patches: 500x500 HR pixels (1,000x1,000 km wind patches; 2,000x2,000 km solar patches), 100x100 MR pixels, 10x10 or 20x20 LR pixels.
N_train: WIND Toolkit (wind): 37,972 examples; NSRDB (solar): 45,109 examples (Table 1). (Total patches extracted before validation split: 42,355 wind / 50,075 solar, of which ~10% withheld for validation per text in Data and Methodology.)
N_eval: WIND Toolkit held-out test: 4,383 examples; NSRDB held-out test: 4,966 examples (Table 1). CCSM4 application/evaluation data: 7,300 daily time steps (2020-2039), for which no ground-truth HR data exist (Table 1, "Application to Climate Data" section).
Leakage notes: The paper states patches are extracted from spatially and temporally continuous WIND Toolkit/NSRDB records (2007-2013, sampled 4-hourly/hourly) and that ~10% of patches are held out for validation, and Table 1 separately reports test-set sizes, but it never explicitly describes whether the train/validation/test partition was made by spatially disjoint regions, by disjoint time periods, or by random sampling of patches mixing both dimensions - so possible spatiotemporal leakage between splits cannot be ruled out or confirmed.
Q1a notes (metric used): Relative MSE of generated u/v (Table 2) and DNI/DHI (Table 3) vs. ground truth is reported as numeric values for bicubic/pretrained-CNN/adversarial methods. Semivariograms of spatial autocorrelation (Fig. 8) are computed as a quantified statistic with error bars (SD across test data) comparing LR, HR, and SR fields.
Q1b notes: Kinetic energy spectrum (Fig. 4, upper) is compared to the theoretical Kolmogorov k^-5/3 line only via a log-log plot with prose interpretation ("providing a visible benefit at the highest wave numbers") - no numeric slope-fit or spectral distance is reported. Velocity-gradient PDF and its expected ~-0.5 skewness (Fig. 4, lower) are likewise assessed only by visual comparison to a Gaussian reference and prose claims ("in much better agreement with the ground truth," "achieving the negative skewness") without a reported computed skewness value per method.
Q1c notes: Turbulent kinetic energy spectrum vs. wavenumber is shown (Fig. 4, upper) with the Kolmogorov -5/3 scaling as a dashed reference line; comparison is qualitative/visual only, no quantitative spectral-slope fit or error statistic is reported.
Q1d notes: Velocity-gradient PDF tails/heavy-tailed behavior and expected negative skewness (turbulence intermittency) are explicitly discussed as a distinct check beyond bulk mean/variance (Fig. 4, lower; "Results, SR of Wind Data"), but only visually/qualitatively (no numeric tail statistics, extreme-quantile comparison, or exceedance analysis). The solar semivariogram "nugget" (small-scale discontinuity from cloud cover) is also examined but again mainly described qualitatively.
Q2a notes: Per-example fidelity between the SR output conditioned on a matched LR input and the corresponding true HR field is shown qualitatively (Figs. 3, 7) and quantitatively via relative MSE (Tables 2-3), which is inherently a conditional accuracy measure. However there is no systematic per-condition breakdown (e.g. by wind-speed regime), no proper scoring rule (CRPS), and no rank/PIT or spread-error analysis, since the network produces a single deterministic realization per LR input rather than a probabilistic ensemble.
Q2b notes: The generator is a deterministic mapping given a fixed LR input (no stochastic ensemble of outputs per condition is generated for calibration purposes); the 1,000-member noise-corruption experiment (Fig. 5) is a robustness/stability test on perturbed inputs, not a probabilistic ensemble used for rank histogram/PIT/spread-error calibration.
Q3 notes: No explicit check of physical admissibility of individual generated samples (e.g., non-negativity of DNI/DHI, physically plausible wind-speed bounds, conservation properties) is reported; validation is limited to aggregate statistical/turbulence properties (spectra, PDFs, semivariograms, MSE) rather than per-sample constraint checking.
Q4a notes (metric used): The noise-robustness study (Fig. 5) computes a variance map of SR output deviations across 1,000 noise-corrupted realizations of the same LR input, which is a quantitative measure of output spread, but it is framed and used solely to demonstrate robustness/stability to input noise, not to assess diversity or mode coverage of the model's conditional distribution.
Q4b notes: No nearest-neighbor-to-training-set or memorization check is reported anywhere in the paper.
Q5a notes: The GAN's discriminator and its loss value (~0.5 target) are discussed only as part of the adversarial training dynamics/balance procedure (Data and Methodology), not deployed as a post-hoc two-sample classifier test on held-out real vs. generated data for evaluation purposes.
Q5b notes: Although renewable energy resource assessment is the stated motivating application, no downstream task metric (e.g., computed wind/solar power output error, train-on-synthetic-test-on-real evaluation) is actually measured; the CCSM "deployment" results (Figs. 6, 9) are shown only as illustrative fields, not evaluated against any downstream resource-assessment ground truth.
V1 notes: Two loosely related checks exist: (1) bicubic interpolation is used as a known-degenerate/over-smoothed baseline, and the spectral/PDF/semivariogram metrics are shown to correctly register it as physically wrong (flat spectrum, Gaussian PDF, no nugget), which functions as an implicit sensitivity/non-gameability check on the metrics; (2) the noise-corruption robustness test (Fig. 5) perturbs the LR input and quantifies (mean, variance) how the SR output changes. Neither is framed explicitly as a formal metric-validity control.
U1 notes: The semivariogram plot (Fig. 8) reports error bars representing the SD across the NSRDB test data for each lag distance, giving an uncertainty estimate on this evaluation statistic. The noise-robustness experiment (Fig. 5) also reports mean and variance across 1,000 noise realizations.
U2 notes: No real-vs-real "floor" baseline (e.g., split-half comparison of real HR data, or a sampling-noise floor) is computed; the "Ground Truth" curve in Fig. 8 is simply the real-data statistic used as the reference, not a real-vs-real comparison.
B1 notes: Bicubic interpolation is included throughout as the non-ML naive baseline (Table 2, Table 3, Figs. 3, 7), compared against the pretrained-CNN and adversarial (GAN) SR outputs.
R1 notes: "Software for the trained networks as well as some example data are available on GitHub at https://github.com/NREL/PhIRE" (Data Availability statement, and Significance/abstract footnotes, ref. 14).
R2 notes: Training protocol is described in reasonable detail (epoch counts, training hours, adaptive discriminator-loss thresholds of 0.6/0.45, patch counts) and the noise-robustness test specifies 1,000 realizations at 5% variance Gaussian noise. However, no random seeds are given, and the exact procedure for constructing the train/validation/test split (needed to reproduce which examples the reported evaluation metrics were computed on) is not fully specified.
Notable practices (free text): The paper grounds its wind-field validation in established turbulence physics (Kolmogorov k^-5/3 kinetic-energy spectrum and velocity-gradient-PDF skewness/heavy tails), a domain-appropriate practice, and uses semivariograms with SD error bars to assess spatial autocorrelation for solar fields, explicitly acknowledging that solar irradiance lacks an equivalent theoretical validation framework. It also runs a genuine robustness/sensitivity test by corrupting LR inputs with Gaussian noise across 1,000 realizations and mapping the resulting output mean/variance. However, all the physically-motivated distributional checks (spectra, PDF shape/skewness) are ultimately reported only as visual plot comparisons with prose claims rather than quantified statistics, and the paper has no diversity/mode-coverage metric, no memorization check, no post-hoc discriminative two-sample test, no per-sample physical-bounds check, and no downstream (e.g., power-output) validation despite that being the paper's stated motivation; the flagship CCSM "50x global downscaling" application (Figs. 6, 9) has no ground truth at all and is validated purely qualitatively.
Memorable unquantified-similarity quotes: "This SR qualitatively appears to be the most comparable with the true HR data. Further, the small structures inserted by the GANs exhibit similar patterns and flow directionality as those found in the true data." (Results, "SR of Wind Data," p. 16811). "The former shows that the GANs generate a wind velocity field perceptually similar to, but not necessarily identical to, the corresponding true HR data." (Discussion, p. 16813).
QC method applied: Per-paper adversarial verify (model_family/Q4a/Q4b/U2/V1/eligibility) — papers_second_batch

Filename: 2021 Bahtia - ExGAN Adversarial Generation of Extreme Samples.pdf
Title: ExGAN: Adversarial Generation of Extreme Samples
Venue: The Thirty-Fifth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-21)
Model family (as reported): Conditional GAN — specifically a conditional DCGAN (ExGAN), built on a DCGAN backbone, combined with a novel "Distribution Shifting" training procedure and EVT (Generalized Pareto Distribution)-based conditioning on an extremeness statistic; baseline is an unconditional DCGAN with EVT-based rejection sampling.
Variable(s): Daily total precipitation (rainfall accumulation), a single-variable 2D spatial field; "extremeness" is operationalized as the total rainfall summed over the whole image, used as the scalar conditioning/measure variable.
Data source: US precipitation dataset from the National Weather Service multi-sensor precipitation estimate (https://water.weather.gov/precip/) — an observational/analysis gridded daily precipitation product (not a climate-model simulation) covering the lower-48 US, Puerto Rico, and Alaska at roughly 4x4 km resolution.
Grid size: Original images 813 x 1051 pixels, resized to 64 x 64 for modeling (source data ~4x4 km resolution, daily).
N_train: Not stated as an explicit count. Training set is daily precipitation images for Jan 2010-Dec 2016 (~7 years, implying roughly 2500+ daily images), but the paper never gives an exact sample count.
N_eval: Not stated as an explicit count. Test period is Jan 2017-Aug 2020, restricted to daily images whose total rainfall exceeds the 95th percentile of the training set; exact number of retained test images is not reported.
Leakage notes: Training data (Jan 2010-Dec 2016) and test data (Jan 2017-Aug 2020) are non-overlapping calendar periods, so the split is a clean forward-in-time temporal split; each sample is a full spatial snapshot for one day, so there is no spatial subsetting/leakage concern within the split. Test set is further restricted to samples exceeding the 95th percentile of the training set's total rainfall.
Q1a notes (metric used): FID is reported quantitatively (mean ± std over 5 runs, with a two-sample t-test p-value of 0.002 for ExGAN vs DCGAN improvement, Table 1), but it is computed via Frechet distance between activations of a custom autoencoder's bottleneck layer (since ImageNet-Inception is unsuitable for this domain), not a direct distributional comparison of the physical variable (rainfall) itself, e.g. no histogram/PDF/KS-test comparison of rainfall values. Reconstruction loss and MAPE (Eq. 2-4) are per-sample fidelity/conditioning-accuracy metrics rather than full-distribution comparisons.
Q1b notes: Section 5.1 "Realistic Samples (Visual Inspection)" shows generated images (Fig. 3) alongside real extreme samples (Fig. 2b) and asserts similarity purely from visual inspection, with no quantification in that subsection: "We observe that ExGAN generates samples that are similar to the images of rainfall patterns from the original data... The typical pattern of radially decreasing rainfall in real data is learned by ExGAN."
Q1c notes: No spatial power spectrum, wavenumber analysis, or any spectral comparison is reported anywhere in the paper.
Q1d notes: The entire method targets the tail: EVT/GPD fitting to the extremeness statistic, conditioning accuracy (MAPE) evaluated down to extremeness probabilities as low as 0.0001 (Fig. 3, Table 3), and reconstruction loss computed specifically on a held-out test set restricted to samples exceeding the 95th percentile of the training set's total rainfall (Section 5, "Dataset"). This is a paper explicitly about generating and evaluating tail/extreme behavior, not just bulk statistics.
Q2a notes: MAPE (Eq. 4) directly measures per-sample conditional fidelity: the discrepancy between the extremeness value used to condition generation (e) and the realized extremeness E(G(z,e)) of the generated sample, reported across multiple extremeness probabilities in Table 2 and Section 5.2 (e.g. "MAPE for ExGAN is 3.14% ± 3.08%").
Q2b notes: No rank histogram, PIT, spread-error, or reliability diagram is computed; the model is not evaluated as a probabilistic ensemble forecast, only as point-conditional sample generation accuracy (MAPE) and image fidelity (FID/reconstruction loss).
Q3 notes: No explicit check of non-negativity, physical bounds, or conservation properties of generated rainfall fields is reported. The closest statement is an informal, unquantified visual observation that "the typical pattern of radially decreasing rainfall... is learned" and "coastal areas are more susceptible to heavy rainfall," which is a qualitative spatial-pattern remark, not an admissibility check.
Q4a notes (metric used): No quantitative diversity/coverage metric (e.g., precision/recall for generative models, mode coverage, pairwise sample distance) is reported anywhere in the paper.
Q4b notes: No nearest-neighbor-to-training-set or other memorization check is performed anywhere in the paper.
Q5a notes: No discriminative classifier-based two-sample test (C2ST) is used; FID (a Frechet distance on autoencoder features) is the only distributional metric, which is a different construct.
Q5b notes: The paper motivates stress-testing/flood-planning use cases in the introduction and conclusion but never actually runs a downstream task (e.g., train-on-synthetic/test-on-real, or a flood-planning task metric) using the generated samples.
V1 notes: No sensitivity check (e.g. testing whether FID/MAPE degrade appropriately for corrupted/perturbed inputs) or non-gameability control (e.g., comparison to a degenerate/statistic-matched null generator) is reported for any of the evaluation metrics.
U1 notes: Table 1 and Table 2 report FID, reconstruction loss, and MAPE as mean ± std averaged over 5 runs, and Table 1 additionally reports a two-sample t-test p-value (0.002) for the significance of ExGAN's FID improvement over DCGAN.
U2 notes: No real-vs-real reference/floor metric (e.g., split-half comparison of the real test set, or sampling-noise baseline) is computed anywhere.
B1 notes: No non-ML baseline (e.g., climatology, persistence, analog method, statistical downscaling) is included. The only baseline is DCGAN (an unconditional GAN) combined with EVT-based rejection sampling — itself a deep generative ML method, not a statistical/climatological baseline.
R1 notes: "Reproducibility: Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Stream-AD/ExGAN" (end of Introduction, p.6753).
R2 notes: Reasonable hyperparameter/procedural detail is given (100 epochs per distribution-shift iteration, c=0.75/k=10 with warm start, reconstruction-loss optimization: latent initialized to zero, lr=0.001, 2000 Adam steps, all metrics averaged over 5 runs), but no explicit random seed values are stated, and the paper repeatedly refers to Appendices A/B/C (experimental setup, network architecture, software) and Appendix E (ablation) for further detail that are not included in this file, so full evaluation reproducibility cannot be fully confirmed from the main text alone.
Notable practices (free text): The paper's core methodological contribution (Distribution Shifting + EVT/GPD-based conditional generation) is explicitly designed to target and quantify tail behavior rather than bulk statistics — it reports a conditioning-accuracy metric (MAPE) down to extremeness probability 0.0001 and a reconstruction-loss test specifically on held-out extreme (>95th percentile) test samples, which is unusually tail-focused for a GAN paper. It also reports mean±std over 5 runs and a t-test p-value for the main FID comparison, which is more rigorous uncertainty reporting than typical for this era. On the weaker side: the FID substitute relies on a small custom autoencoder (since ImageNet-Inception features are inappropriate for this domain) whose validity as a metric is never checked for sensitivity or gameability; there is no diversity/mode-coverage metric, no memorization/nearest-neighbor check against training images (a notable gap given GANs' known tendency to memorize in low-data extreme-tail regimes), no discriminative two-sample test, and no non-ML baseline.
Memorable unquantified-similarity quotes: "We observe that ExGAN generates samples that are similar to the images of rainfall patterns from the original data in Figure 2b... The typical pattern of radially decreasing rainfall in real data is learned by ExGAN. ExGAN also learns that coastal areas are more susceptible to heavy rainfall." (Section 5.1, "Realistic Samples (Visual Inspection)", p.6755)

Title: A generative adversarial network approach to (ensemble) weather prediction
Venue: Neural Networks 139 (2021) 1-16 (Elsevier)
Model family (as reported): Conditional GAN (cGAN) - pix2pix/vid2vid-style architecture with a 3D U-Net generator (ConvLSTM bottleneck) and PatchGAN discriminator; stochasticity/ensembling via Monte-Carlo dropout at train and test time
Variable(s): 500 hPa geopotential height, 2-meter temperature, total precipitation (three separate univariate cGAN models, each trained on one variable alone)
Data source: ERA5 reanalysis (ECMWF), via Copernicus Climate Change Service (CCCS, 2017)
Grid size: 128 x 128 grid points (downsampled from original 240x240 at 0.25 deg x 0.25 deg to ~0.5 deg x 0.5 deg resolution), domain 30N-90N, 30W-30E over Europe
N_train: Not stated as an explicit sample/sequence count; described as 4 years (2015-2018) of ERA5 data at 3-hourly resolution
N_eval: Not stated as an explicit sample/sequence count; described as 1 year (2019) of ERA5 data at 3-hourly resolution
Leakage notes: Training data spans 2015-2018 and test data is entirely 2019, a temporally distinct block, with no shuffling across the boundary described. This constitutes explicit temporal block separation, consistent with standard weather-forecast verification practice, even though there is no explicit buffer gap between the last training timestamp and the first test timestamp.
Q1a notes (metric used): The paper reports point-wise skill metrics (RMSE, ACC, CRPS) as functions of forecast lead time (Figs. 3-4), but never computes a distance/divergence between the marginal or joint distribution of generated field values and the true distribution (no KS-test, Wasserstein distance, energy score, or histogram comparison of overall value distributions).
Q1b notes: No histogram or PDF overlay of generated vs. true field-value distributions appears anywhere. Qualitative similarity claims in case studies ("excellent agreement", "reasonably well") concern spatial-map comparisons of individual forecast instances (Figs. 5-15), not distribution/histogram overlays, so this specific criterion does not apply.
Q1c notes: No spatial spectral analysis (power spectrum, wavenumber decomposition) is reported anywhere in the paper.
Q1d notes: Two of the three case studies specifically target extreme/rare events (post-tropical storm Lorenzo, Sec. 4.2.1; severe convective outbreak after storm Miguel, Sec. 4.2.2), which the author notes are "by definition rare and thus not sufficiently represented in the training data" (p.8). However these are evaluated via the same visual spatial-map comparison and general aggregate skill scores used for bulk statistics, not via dedicated tail/extreme-value quantitative metrics (no exceedance-probability scores, no extreme-quantile verification).
Q2a notes: CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) is computed for the 100-member Monte-Carlo-dropout ensemble as a function of forecast lead time for all three variables (Fig. 4, Sec. 4.1), comparing the ensemble predictive CDF to the observed value at each time. RMSE and ACC are also reported per lead time (Fig. 3).
Q2b notes: No rank histogram, PIT histogram, or reliability diagram is computed. CRPS is reported (a combined calibration+sharpness proper score) but not decomposed into a calibration component. Spread-error correspondence is discussed only qualitatively through case studies (e.g., comparing ensemble-stdev maps to plausible error regions, or noting smaller spread at Lisbon vs. larger at Milan, Sec. 4.2.2), and the author explicitly states "we reserve a more careful calibration of the ensemble prediction model to future studies" (Sec. 3.3, p.6).
Q3 notes: No explicit check of physical admissibility of individual generated samples is reported (e.g., no verification that generated precipitation is non-negative, no conservation checks, no structural/bounds constraints tested), despite precipitation being a strictly non-negative quantity.
Q4a notes (metric used): Point-wise ensemble standard deviation (z_std) is computed over 100 Monte-Carlo-dropout realizations of each vid2vid model, quantifying spread/diversity among generated samples at each grid point/time (Sec. 3.3), and is mapped throughout the case studies (Figs. 5-15). However this diversity measure is used to characterize forecast uncertainty rather than validated against a real-world diversity reference; the author notes the spread magnitude has no a priori known relationship to true atmospheric uncertainty and requires an unverified, experimentally-chosen scaling factor γ=10 (Sec. 3.3).
Q4b notes: No nearest-neighbor-to-training-set or memorization check is performed anywhere in the paper.
Q5a notes: No classifier-based two-sample test (C2ST) is performed on held-out generated vs. real fields. The PatchGAN discriminator is used only internally during adversarial training, not as a post-hoc evaluation tool on the test set.
Q5b notes: No downstream-task utility evaluation (e.g., train-on-synthetic-test-on-real, augmentation gain) is reported.
V1 notes: No sensitivity check (verifying a metric degrades appropriately on a corrupted/degenerate forecast) or non-gameability check (e.g., statistic-matched null baseline) is reported for any evaluation metric used.
U1 notes: All reported metrics (RMSE, ACC, CRPS) are given as point estimates (e.g., annual means in Fig. 3, lead-time curves in Fig. 4) without confidence intervals, error bars, or bootstrap/resampling-based uncertainty on the metrics themselves.
U2 notes: No real-vs-real reference/floor quantity (e.g., sampling-noise baseline, split-half or inter-annual observation-vs-observation comparison) is computed anywhere; all comparisons are ML-forecast-vs-observation or ML-forecast-vs-ECMWF-NWP.
B1 notes: The ACC metric is explicitly defined relative to a 30-year climatological baseline (z_clim, computed by averaging 1989–2018 ERA5 data by hour-of-day, Sec. 4.1), so ACC=0 corresponds to no skill beyond climatology. In addition, RMSE and ACC of the cGAN forecasts are directly plotted against ECMWF's operational (physics-based) NWP forecast verification scores for geopotential and 2m temperature (Fig. 3), obtained courtesy of an ECMWF scientist per the Acknowledgments.
R1 notes: "The code is available on Github." with link https://github.com/abihlo/vid2vidEra5 (Sec. 3.4, footnote 2).
R2 notes: RMSE, ACC and CRPS formulas are given explicitly (Sec. 4.1); number of ensemble realizations (100), MC-dropout rate (20%), and the ad hoc uncertainty-cone scaling factor (γ=10) are stated; train/test period is explicit (2015-2018 train / 2019 test). However no explicit random seed(s) are reported in the text for reproducing the exact stochastic dropout realizations.
Notable practices (free text): Notable for directly benchmarking cGAN forecasts against standard operational meteorological verification metrics (RMSE, ACC, CRPS) and against real ECMWF operational NWP forecasts and climatology, a level of domain-appropriate quantitative rigor uncommon in generic ML generative-model evaluations. However, the Monte-Carlo-dropout "ensemble" varies only the model (via dropout masks), not the initial conditions, and its spread is rescaled by an experimentally chosen, unverified factor (gamma=10) "to give reasonably well-defined probability cones," with no rank histogram, PIT, or other calibration diagnostic used to check whether this spread is properly calibrated. Physical realism, sample diversity, and memorization are almost exclusively assessed qualitatively through visual inspection of a handful of case-study maps (hurricane Lorenzo, storm Miguel) with prose claims of "excellent"/"reasonable" agreement rather than dedicated quantitative or held-out statistical tests. The author is commendably candid about limitations, explicitly noting that comparing the model's ensemble CRPS against a true NWP ensemble "would be misleading" since only the model, not the initial conditions, is perturbed.
Memorable unquantified-similarity quotes: "Visually these forecasts agree reasonably well, with the most interesting feature being high values of uncertainty forecast over the Baltic states, Poland, Hungary, Slovenia, Croatia and Northern Italy, as well as over Portugal and Spain." (Sec. 4.2.2, p.9) / "As in the previous case, the model shows an excellent agreement with the true evolution of the 500 hPa geopotential height surface on this day." (Sec. 4.2.2, p.9) / "The vid2vid model can capture this evolution both qualitatively and quantitatively reasonably well..." (Sec. 4.2.1, p.8, stated without any per-case quantitative metric accompanying this specific claim).

Filename: 2021 Ravuri - Skilful precipitation nowcasting using deep generative models of radar.pdf
Title: Skilful precipitation nowcasting using deep generative models of radar
Venue: Nature (Vol 597, 30 September 2021, pp. 672-677)
Model family (as reported): Conditional GAN — a spatiotemporal generator with spatial and temporal convolutional discriminators plus a grid-cell regularization term (the authors' own name: "Deep Generative Model of Rainfall", DGMR)
Variable(s): Surface precipitation (rain) rate, mm/h, derived from radar reflectivity composites; quantized in 1/32 mm/h increments; capped at 128 mm/h for training.
Data source: Observational radar composites: Met Office RadarNet4 network (UK, 2016-2019, 5-min, 1 km resolution, quality-controlled with orographic enhancement and rain-gauge mean-field adjustment); secondary generalization dataset: NOAA Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) composites for the USA (2017-2019).
Grid size: Native 1 km x 1 km resolution; UK domain up to 1,536 x 1,280 grid cells (1,536 km x 1,280 km); training crops 256x256; evaluation crops 512x512 (scored on centre 64x64 cells to avoid boundary effects); US domain: three 1,536x1,536 regions (Pacific NW, Midwest, Northeast)
N_train: ~1.5 million training examples (256x256 crops, after importance sampling to oversample heavy precipitation), UK radar 2016-2018; US model trained on 2 years of MRMS data.
N_eval: UK yearly test set: subsampled to 66,851 crops (512x512) for CSI/CRPS/correlation/economic-value metrics; full-frame 2019 predictions used for PSD; weekly-split test = 36,106 examples; US test = 1 year of MRMS (2019). Expert study: 56 meteorologists, each rating a unique set of 20 nowcasts (10 medium->5mm/h, 10 heavy->10mm/h) drawn from a corpus of 2,126 high-intensity 2019 events, plus 3 shared case-study events rated by all 56; 10 of the 56 took part in follow-up phase-2 interviews.
Leakage notes: Training uses 2016-2018 (with first-of-month days from that period reserved for validation) and testing uses the entirely separate year 2019 ("preventing data leakage and testing for out of distribution generalization", Methods/UK dataset). An alternative weekly split (Thu-Mon train / Tue val / Wed test) is also tested for generalization. Given the yearly separation vastly exceeds precipitation's spatiotemporal autocorrelation scale (hours to days), this is not leakage-prone.
Q1a notes (metric used): The paper's quantitative suite (CSI, CRPS, Pearson correlation, relative economic value) is built around forecast-accuracy/skill scores rather than a standalone marginal-distribution comparison (e.g. histogram/CDF/Wasserstein distance of rain-rate values) between generated and real fields. CRPS is a proper scoring rule that does quantify distributional fidelity of the predictive ensemble against real outcomes (Fig. 3, pooled at 1/4/16 km), which partially satisfies this criterion, but it is conditioned per-event/location rather than an unconditional distributional match. The closest true "distribution of a physical quantity" check is the quantified power spectral density (coded separately under Q1c).
Q1b notes: No purely visual/prose-only distributional comparison was found; every visual similarity claim in the case studies (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Figs. 2-3) is accompanied by CSI/CRPS numbers in the same panel, and the spectral "effective resolution" claims are quantified (32 km, 16 km, etc.), not just visual overlays.
Q1c notes: Radially averaged power spectral density (PSD) is reported for full-frame predictions at multiple lead times (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Figs. 5-9), and the authors derive a quantified "effective resolution" for each model (e.g. "the effective resolution for UNet is 32 km and for axial attention is 16 km" at T+90 min, p.674), directly comparing to observation PSD curves.
Q1d notes: CSI is reported at increasing thresholds (1, 4, 8 mm/h; Fig. 2a), CRPS pooled for maximum (not just average) precipitation rate (Fig. 3b), economic value computed at 5/10/15 mm cumulative-rain thresholds (Fig. 4a), and the expert meteorologist study specifically targets medium (>5 mm/h) and heavy (>10 mm/h) rain events "to make meaningful statements of operational usefulness" (p.675) — extremes are a central, explicit focus, not an afterthought.
Q2a notes: CRPS reported per lead time and per spatial pooling scale (1/4/16 km, Fig. 3), Pearson correlation coefficient across lead times and aggregations (Extended Data Fig. 4c), reliability diagrams and rank histograms at T+60 min (Extended Data Fig. 4d,e) — extensive conditional/probabilistic fidelity evaluation.
Q2b notes: Reliability diagrams and sharpness plots for two precipitation thresholds, and rank histograms at T+60 min are shown (Extended Data Fig. 4d,e; Fig. 9d,e for US), explicitly discussed: "Post-processing improves the reliability diagrams and rank histogram to be as or more skilful than the baseline methods" (p.675).
Q3 notes: No explicit check of individual-sample physical admissibility (non-negativity, mass conservation, structural bounds) for DGMR's own outputs is reported. The one related remark — that Gaussian-process-copula perturbed samples from the axial-attention baseline "were not physically plausible, due to the stationary and unconditional correlation structure" (Methods, Axial attention baseline) — is a qualitative judgment about a competing method's ad hoc post-processing, not a systematic admissibility check of the generative model's own samples.
Q4a notes (metric used): Rank histograms (Extended Data Fig. 4e/9e) and the ensemble-size sensitivity of economic value (1 vs 20 samples, Extended Data Fig. 4b/9b) indirectly reflect ensemble spread/diversity, but these are framed as calibration/value analyses rather than a dedicated diversity or coverage metric (e.g. sample variance vs. truth variance, entropy). "Postage stamp plots to visualize the ensemble variability" are referenced (Supplementary Data 1-3) but described as visualization only, not a quantitative diversity score.
Q4b notes: No nearest-neighbor-to-training-set or memorization check of any kind is mentioned anywhere in the main text, methods, or extended data.
Q5a notes: The spatial/temporal discriminators are used only as part of the adversarial training objective (Eq. 2/4/5), not as an independent post-hoc classifier-based two-sample test used for evaluation/reporting.
Q5b notes: Relative economic value is computed using a cost/loss decision-analytic model (Richardson 2000) across three rain-accumulation thresholds (Fig. 4a) — a genuine downstream decision-utility metric. In addition, a large blinded expert-meteorologist study (n=56) directly assessed operational usefulness/decision value via ranked preference and structured interviews (Fig. 4b-d), grounding the economic analysis in real-world task performance.
V1 notes: The paper explicitly flags metric gameability: "standard metrics implicitly assume that models... preserve the physical plausibility of forecasts, [but] deep learning systems may outperform on certain metrics by failing to satisfy other needed characteristics" (p.673), motivating PSD specifically because it is sensitive to blur/degeneracy that CSI/CRPS miss (demonstrated by UNet/axial-attention's collapsed "effective resolution" of 32/16 km, p.674). The ablation note that discriminator-only losses "lead to accuracy on par with Eulerian persistence" is also a sensitivity check against a degenerate baseline.
U1 notes: Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence intervals reported on meteorologist first-choice proportions (Fig. 4c,d: 89% [0.86,0.92], 90% [0.87,0.92]); paired permutation tests with alternating weeks as independent units (n=26) and 10^6 permutations report explicit P-values (P<10^-4, P<10^-3) for CSI/CRPS/preference comparisons throughout (Methods, "Quantitative evaluation").
U2 notes: Fig. 2b/Extended Data Figs. 5-9 plot "Obs. 1 km" against the same real radar observations coarsened to the blurry models' inferred resolutions (e.g. "Obs. 8 km", "Obs. 32 km", "Obs. 16 km") — a real-vs-real (real vs. coarsened-real) spectral reference used as the floor/benchmark for interpreting each model's effective resolution.
B1 notes: PySTEPS (an advection/optical-flow ensemble nowcasting system, "considered to be state-of-the-art") is used as a non-ML baseline throughout, and an NWP (UKV deterministic forecast) is also compared against in Extended Data Fig. 5, showing "NWPs are not competitive in this regime." Eulerian persistence is also referenced as a sanity-check baseline in the ablation discussion.
R1 notes: "We have also released a pretrained version of the generative model available at github.com/deepmind/deepmind-research/tree/master/nowcasting," along with pseudocode (pseudocode.py) in the Supplementary Information (Code availability section, p.677).
R2 notes: Evaluation protocol is described in substantial procedural detail: subsampling/importance-sampling scheme for the test set (66,851 crops), centre-crop scoring to avoid boundary effects, algorithmic crop-selection procedure for the meteorologist study, number of permutations for significance tests (10^6 for permutation tests, 10,000 resamplings for CIs), ensemble sizes (20 samples), and full ethics/consent protocol for the human study. However, no explicit numeric random seeds are given for model sampling or bootstrap procedures.
Notable practices (free text): Unusually rigorous, multi-pronged evaluation for a generative-model paper: quantitative deterministic (CSI) and probabilistic (pooled CRPS at 1/4/16 km) verification, quantified spectral "effective resolution" specifically designed to expose the blurring failure mode of competing deep-learning baselines, decision-theoretic economic value analysis (cost/loss model), and a large (n=56), ethically-approved, blinded/randomized expert-meteorologist ranking + structured-interview study with bootstrapped/permutation-based significance testing and Clopper-Pearson CIs. The authors explicitly warn that standard verification scores and expert judgments of realism/utility are not always aligned, i.e. that popular metrics can be "gamed" by blurry, non-physical predictions. Weaknesses: no sample-level physical-admissibility check, no memorization/nearest-neighbor check, and no dedicated diversity/coverage metric distinct from calibration (rank histograms serve a dual calibration/spread role); ensemble "postage stamp" diversity visualizations are qualitative only.
Memorable unquantified-similarity quotes: "By comparison, DGMR preserves a good spatial envelope, represents the convection and maintains heavy rainfall in the early prediction, although with less accurate rates at T + 90 min and at the edge of the radar than at previous time steps." (p.673, Intercomparison case study — a visual/qualitative characterization, though CSI/CRPS numbers appear alongside in Fig. 1). Also, from the phase-2 meteorologist interviews (p.677): "Meteorologists described DGMR as having the 'best envelope', 'representing the risk best', as having 'much higher detail compared to what [expert meteorologists] are used to at the moment', and as capturing 'both the size of convection cells and intensity the best'" — purely qualitative realism descriptors (part of a quantified preference study overall, but the individual testimonial claims themselves carry no attached metric).

Filename: 2022 Boulaguiem - Modeling and simulating spatial extremes by combining extreme value theory with generative adversarial networks.pdf
Title: Modeling and simulating spatial extremes by combining extreme value theory with generative adversarial networks
Venue: Environmental Data Science (Cambridge University Press), 2022, 1: e5
Model family (as reported): GAN — specifically a DCGAN (deep convolutional GAN) trained on copula-transformed (uniform-margin) block maxima, combined with univariate extreme value theory (GEV marginal fitting); the authors term the combined pipeline "evtGAN".
Variable(s): Summer temperature annual maxima (Kelvin) and winter precipitation annual maxima (meter/day), each an annual block-maximum spatial field over 1822 grid points.
Data source: 2000-year stationary large-ensemble simulation with the EC-Earth v2.3 global climate model, representative of present-day climate (GMST matched to 2011-2015 HadCRUT4); 16 transient runs x 25 ensemble members x 5-year time slice = 2000 years of daily data at T159 (~1°) resolution.
Grid size: 18 x 22 grid points (1822 total), ~1 degree (T159) resolution, western Europe domain
N_train: 50 (main experiment); sensitivity analysis also run with n_train = 30 and 100 (Figure 8)
N_eval: Test set = all remaining years after the 50 used for training: 1950 samples for temperature (2000 total years) and 1949 for precipitation (1999 total years); explicitly stated as "the test set (1950 samples)" in Section 3.3.
Leakage notes: The model is fit only on a 50-observation training set and evaluated against a disjoint remainder used as test set ("Both methods are fitted using only the training data set and the evaluation is made considering the information contained in the test set as ground truth," Section 3). Each observation is an annual block maximum (summer temperature max / winter precipitation max) over the full spatial domain; the paper explicitly motivates using block maxima instead of raw daily data because it "does not suffer from serial correlation and seasonality issues" (Section 1, p. e5-3), reducing autocorrelation-driven leakage risk between train and test years. However, the exact assignment of years to the 50-observation training set (random subsample of the 2000 years vs. a contiguous block) is not stated.
Q1a notes (metric used): Figure 8 quantifies the mean l2 norm between vectors of extremal correlations (chi) computed from evtGAN samples versus the train set (Ctr) and versus the test set (Cte), tracked across training epochs (1 to 30,000) and across three training sample sizes (n=30, 50, 100) separately for temperature and precipitation. This is a genuine scalar divergence metric on a tail-dependence statistic, not a purely visual comparison.
Q1b notes: Bivariate joint distributions (Figures 4-5) are compared via density scatterplots with prose claims such as "Purely based on visual judgment, it seems that evtGAN is able to characterize the different tail dependencies relatively well" (Section 3.3, p. e5-10). Extremal-correlation scatter plots against the 1:1 line (Figure 6) and spectral (angular) distribution KDE overlays against test-set histograms (Figure 7) are likewise assessed by eye/prose ("evtGAN...estimates are very close to the ground truth", "Brown–Resnick...fails completely for the remaining three cases") without an accompanying divergence number for these specific comparisons (only the extremal-correlation summary in Figure 8 is separately quantified).
Q1c notes: No spatial power/Fourier spectrum of the fields is reported. The paper's "spectral distribution" (Figure 7) is the extreme-value-theory angular/spectral measure H(x) describing the extremal dependence angle between pairs of locations at a 0.95 threshold — a tail-dependence concept, not a spatial-frequency spectrum of the generated fields.
Q1d notes: The entire evaluation targets extremes specifically: GEV marginal parameters (location/scale/shape, Figure 3), bivariate extremal correlation chi (Figures 4, 6, 8), and the extremal angular/spectral distribution H(x) at a 0.95 threshold (Figure 7) — all well beyond bulk statistics like mean/variance.
Q2a notes: The model is unconditional: the generator maps latent noise Y directly to a full spatial field of block maxima, with no conditioning input/predictor, so per-condition conditional fidelity metrics do not apply.
Q2b notes: Unconditional model with no ensemble-vs-observation conditioning setup; no rank histogram/PIT/spread-error/reliability diagram is applicable or reported.
Q3 notes: No check of physical admissibility of individual generated samples (e.g., non-negativity of precipitation values, physically plausible temperature bounds, spatial smoothness/structural constraints) is reported; only population-level marginal and extremal statistics are examined.
Q4a notes (metric used): No quantitative diversity/coverage metric (e.g., precision-recall for generative models, sample variance ratio, mode counting) is computed. The qualitative point that DCGAN samples remain "bounded to the range of the train set" (Section 4, p. e5-13) touches on limited extrapolation/diversity but is shown only via scatterplot panels (Figures 4d,i,n; 5d,i,n), not quantified.

(Section 5.2, p.14).

Q4a notes (metric used): Table 2 explicitly labels W1,r/c and SWDmulti as "Diversity" metrics ("Purpose: Diversity"); these EMD-based distances quantify whether GAN samples span the same spread as AROME-EPS, and multivariate-ablation experiments (Section 5) explicitly discuss diversity trade-offs quantified via these same metrics, e.g. "the largest distributional discrepancy of Config. 1 even hints at some form of mode collapse."

B1 notes: No non-ML baseline (climatology, persistence, analog, statistical downscaling) is included. R1 notes: "The code used to train networks and analyze data through all metrics can be found at https://github.com/flyIchtus/multivariate-GAN" (Data availability statement). The AROME-EPS dataset itself is stated to be released later ("will be made available at the end of the ANR project").

(Section 4b(1), "Visual examination"); "First, the resolution of GAN-produced samples appears to be correct when compared to AROME-EPS outputs. Q2b notes: Case-study Figs. 7-8 show histograms/KDEs of the 64-member forecast ensemble with the observed value marked, offering an ad hoc visual spread-vs-truth check for 3 storms only, not a systematic PIT/rank histogram or reliability diagram over the full test set. "In general, the structural forecast follows the observed profile, even at 12-h lead times" (pp. 991-992, sec. 4a(2)).

Q1c notes: No spatial/spectral analysis is applicable or reported for this RGB land-cover classification context.
Q1d notes: No tail/extreme-case evaluation is performed; this is a classification-oriented image augmentation study without a continuous physical variable whose extremes would be assessed.
Q2a notes: No direct per-sample check that generated images match their conditioning class/prompt (e.g., no classifier-based prompt-fidelity score applied to the synthetic images themselves); downstream classification accuracy gains serve only as an indirect, aggregate signal of conditional fidelity.
